title: The House on the Borderland
author: William Hope Hodgson
written: 1907, in the burst of work that followed Hodgson's years at sea
setting: A grey stone house above a pit in the west of Ireland, and then the whole of space and time seen from its study window
lengthNote: A frame, an introduction and twenty-seven short chapters, about 54,000 words, with an editor's footnotes and a manuscript that stops in the middle of a word
openingLine: Many are the hours in which I have pondered upon the story that is set forth in the following pages.
summary: Two anglers in the west of Ireland find a ruined house above a chasm and a damp manuscript in the rubble. It was written by a man who lived there alone with his sister and his dog, and it describes two things: a siege by swine-faced creatures that come up out of the pit, and a set of visions in which the writer sits in his own chair while the sun races across the sky, slows, dies, and goes out. The second half is one of the strangest passages in English fiction — no plot, no dialogue, one man watching the solar system end — and it stops mid-word.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The House on the Borderland (eBook 10002)
sourceText.note: The 1908 text, with Hodgson's spellings, his dedication to his father, and the sixteen footnotes signed Ed. that the fictional editor adds to the manuscript.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Dated December 1907 at the end of the author's introduction.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Published by Chapman & Hall, the second of the four novels Hodgson brought out in five years.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Found by two anglers, printed with an editor's footnotes, and broken off mid-word at the end.

atAGlance.label: Reputation
atAGlance.note: He called the cosmic sweep of the second half a classic of the first water, and took the method from it.

structure.label: The frame
structure.title: Two anglers, a ruin and a damp book
structure.summary: Hodgson spends his opening pages establishing how the story reaches us: a fishing holiday in Kraighten, a village with no road to it, a house reduced to rubble above a pit, and a small thick book dug out of the debris. The narrator who reads it warns that the account is stiff and abrupt and that he has left it alone, which licenses everything strange that follows.

scenes.title: The pit-water smell
scenes.summary: The editor describes handling the manuscript: damp pages, close handwriting, and the last few leaves blank.

scenes.title: Kraighten
scenes.summary: Two men fish a river in the west of Ireland, find a garden gone wild and a house thrown down, and dig the book out of the wreck.

structure.label: The first vision
structure.title: A green jade house, in an arena of gods
structure.summary: The Recluse is carried out of his body across a plain and into an amphitheatre of mountains, where he finds his own house rebuilt in green jade at enormous scale, ringed by the gods and monsters of every mythology. He is shown it, and not told anything. The vision establishes what the rest of the book assumes: the house stands where two orders of reality touch.

scenes.title: Out of the body
scenes.summary: The first seizure takes him from his study to a silent plain under a red sun.

scenes.title: Built of green jade
scenes.summary: His own house, identical in every particular except colour and size, at the centre of a ring of watching figures.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: He is brought home to find his sister worried and himself unable to explain where he has been.

structure.label: The swine-things
structure.title: The siege by the swine-things
structure.summary: The middle of the novel is a straight siege story and a very good one. Creatures with human bodies and swine faces come out of the chasm, and the Recluse defends the house room by room with a rifle and a barricade while his sister is kept ignorant. Hodgson is exact about ammunition, doors, cellar trapdoors and the sound of things moving underground.

scenes.title: The first one
scenes.summary: A face at the edge of the chasm, and a dog that will not go near it.

scenes.title: The siege begins
scenes.summary: The creatures cross the garden at night; the windows and doors become the plot.

scenes.ref: The Trap in the Great Cellar
scenes.title: Underneath
scenes.summary: The pit runs under the house, and the last defence is a stone slab.

structure.label: The Sea of Sleep
structure.title: Meeting his lost love
structure.summary: Between the siege and the ending, the book turns quiet. The Recluse is taken to a still sea under a vast white orb and meets the woman he loved and lost, and the only tenderness in the novel is here. The darkness that comes across the orb — she calls it the Sun of Darkness — is the same darkness that will end the book.

scenes.title: Together again
scenes.summary: A meeting with no explanation offered and none asked for.

scenes.title: The Sun of Darkness
scenes.summary: The light is eaten across and she has to go before it closes.

structure.label: The end of the solar system
structure.title: The death of the sun
structure.summary: Time accelerates. Days flicker, the sun becomes a band of fire, the years run out, and the Recluse sits in his study while the earth slows, the sun reddens and dies, a green star draws the system into itself, and the last light goes. His dog crumbles to dust beside him. The manuscript ends in the middle of a word, and a footnote observes that the pen has trailed off across the paper.

scenes.title: Days like a heartbeat
scenes.summary: The sun's arc speeds up until light and dark blur into a grey band.

scenes.title: Pulled off course
scenes.summary: A green sun grows in the sky and the earth's orbit begins to change.

scenes.ref: The End of the Solar System
scenes.title: The dead sun
scenes.summary: The sun goes out, the earth travels across its dark face, and the cold arrives.

scenes.title: The last pages
scenes.summary: The Celestial Globes, the Dark Sun, and a sentence that stops.

characters.name: The Recluse
characters.role: The writer of the manuscript, never named
characters.summary: A man who bought a house nobody would live in because it was cheap, keeps no servants, and describes himself as not superstitious on the page before the visions start. He is brave under siege, exact in his descriptions, and entirely alone with what he has seen; the diary exists because there is no one he can tell.
characters.clue: Says the peasantry call him mad, and starts a diary so that readers may say it too.

relationships.label: lives with, protects from the truth

characters.name: Pepper
characters.summary: The only creature the Recluse says he prefers to the rest of creation, and the one that makes the ending land. Through the siege he is the alarm and the company; in the last chapters he sleeps through the acceleration of time and is touched with a foot and falls to pieces. It is the book's cruellest and best-judged paragraph.
characters.clue: Crumbles into a mouldering heap of bones and dust at the nudge of a boot.

characters.name: Mary
characters.summary: She keeps the house, asks few questions, and is kept out of the story by her brother’s decision, not her own. Hodgson uses her to measure how far the Recluse has gone: the more he sees, the less he tells the one person in the building with him.
characters.clue: Is told nothing about the creatures in the garden, and cooks through the siege.

characters.name: The Swine-things
characters.role: What climbs out of the pit
characters.summary: Human in shape and swine in face, they come in numbers, climb walls, and are stopped only by walls and bullets. Hodgson never explains them or connects them to the cosmic material, and that is why they frighten: they stand for nothing.
characters.clue: The first is identified by a single sentence: it was the face of a swine.

characters.name: The woman of the Sea of Sleep
characters.role: The love the Recluse lost before the book began
characters.summary: She appears only in the quiet chapters, on a still sea under a white orb, and is given no history that the reader can hold. Her leaving, forced by a darkness crossing the light, is the emotional rehearsal for the ending, where a bigger darkness takes everything else.
characters.clue: Calls the advancing blackness the Sun of Darkness and goes before it closes.

characters.name: The editor
characters.role: The voice of the frame and the sixteen footnotes
characters.summary: He prints the manuscript, declines to interpret it, and then cannot help himself: the footnotes offer orbital mechanics, speculation about the speed of time, and finally a note on the ink trailing off the page. The apparatus of scholarship applied to the impossible is the book's quietest and best joke.
characters.clue: Signs his notes Ed., and ends the book with a remark about a pen.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: The Recluse keeps no servants, hates his neighbours, protects his sister from the facts and talks only to a dog. The diary exists because of that, and the whole book is the record of a solitude that has no outlet except paper.
themes.development: He begins alone by choice, is besieged alone by necessity, and ends alone in a universe with no other living thing in it.

themes.name: Deep time
themes.summary: Hodgson takes the geological and astronomical timescales that Victorian science had made familiar and puts one man inside them, conscious, in his own study. The horror is a rate, not an event.
themes.development: Days blur into a band, years into a flicker, and by the last chapters the sun is a dead face the earth crawls across.

themes.name: Unexplained horror
themes.summary: No one in the book understands what has happened. The Recluse reports, the editor annotates, and neither offers a cause for the pit, the creatures or the visions.
themes.development: The footnotes get more confident as the events get less explicable, until the last one is reduced to describing the movement of a pen.

themes.name: Religion
themes.summary: The introduction says the story carries a shadowed picture of what may be given the accepted titles of Heaven and Hell, and the arena of gods and the Sea of Sleep supply both. No religion is named and no comfort is offered.
themes.development: The vision of the gods comes early and is never returned to; what the book ends with instead is physics.

themes.name: The pit
themes.summary: The chasm is a real feature of the ground, measured at about a hundred and fifty feet, and it is also the way through. Hodgson gets his effects by treating the supernatural as geology.
themes.development: It is a curiosity in the first chapters, a source in the middle, and by the cellar chapters it is directly under the floor.

themes.name: The damaged manuscript
themes.summary: The text arrives damaged: damp, abrupt, gapped, and finally broken off. Every uncertainty in the story can be blamed on the document, which is exactly why the document is presented so carefully.
themes.development: The frame introduces the damage, the footnotes measure it, and the last word is unfinished.

themes.name: Lost love
themes.summary: The one relationship in the book is with someone lost before it starts, met again only in a vision, and lost a second time to an advancing darkness.
themes.development: The Sea of Sleep chapters supply the loss that the cosmic ending then repeats on the scale of a solar system.

techniques.name: The found manuscript
techniques.definition: A story presented as a document discovered by someone else.
techniques.inThisBook: Two anglers, a ruin and a damp book. The frame lets the second half abandon plot entirely: what we are reading is a record, not a novel, and records can stop.

techniques.name: Withheld explanation
techniques.definition: Refusing to supply causes for the events described.
techniques.inThisBook: Why the house, why the pit, what the swine-things are, who the gods in the arena were — none of it is answered, and nothing in the book behaves as though an answer is owed.

techniques.name: Precise geography
techniques.definition: Description built out of distances, depths and materials.
techniques.inThisBook: The pit is about a hundred and fifty feet deep, the garden has a wall, the cellar has a slab. The cosmic chapters work because the domestic ones were surveyed first.

techniques.name: Symbolic objects
techniques.definition: A single object carrying the book's meaning without being glossed.
techniques.inThisBook: The same house appears in green jade at the centre of an arena of gods, identical in every particular but colour and scale. Hodgson never says what that means and never needs to.

techniques.name: Journal form
techniques.definition: A first-person record composed after the events, under pressure.
techniques.inThisBook: The prose is stiff and abrupt, as the editor warns, and the stiffness is doing work: a man writing this fast has no time to make it literary.

techniques.name: The siege
techniques.definition: An extended action sequence in a fixed location.
techniques.inThisBook: Doors, windows, ammunition, a cellar trap: the middle third is a practical defence story, and the practicality is what keeps the reader for the unreadable wonders on either side of it.

techniques.name: Haunted-house conventions
techniques.definition: An isolated building with a history, bought cheap by a man who should know better.
techniques.inThisBook: Hodgson sets up the full apparatus in two paragraphs — eighty years empty, a bad name, a ridiculous price — and then spends the novel on things the gothic has no vocabulary for.

quotations.text: I read, and, in reading, lifted the Curtains of the Impossible that blind the mind, and looked out into the unknown.
quotations.context: The editor describing his first reading of the manuscript.
quotations.analysis: The book’s promise, made by a character, not the author. Capitalising the Curtains of the Impossible is Edwardian in the worst way and exactly right for a man who has just read something he cannot place.

quotations.text: I have the queer, faint, pit-water smell of it in my nostrils now as I write
quotations.context: Handling the manuscript before printing it.
quotations.analysis: A smell, not a sight, and it belongs to the pit the story will turn on. Hodgson authenticates his document with one physical sensation that the editor cannot get rid of, which is worth more than any amount of insistence that the tale is true.

quotations.text: The peasantry, who inhabit the wilderness beyond, say that I am mad.
quotations.context: The Recluse's first sentences in his own diary.
quotations.analysis: He raises the charge himself, in the third line, and disposes of it by explaining that he simply will not deal with people. The manoeuvre makes him sound reliable and also tells us that the only witness we will get has a reputation.

quotations.text: I have one friend, a dog; yes, I would sooner have old Pepper than the rest of Creation together.
quotations.context: Explaining his household: a sister, no servants, and the dog.
quotations.analysis: Hodgson plants the ending here, two hundred pages early. The rest of Creation is precisely what the last chapters take away, and the reader is told at the start which part of it the Recluse would have kept.

quotations.text: For a couple of centuries, this house has had a reputation, a bad one
quotations.analysis: The whole gothic inheritance, disposed of in a clause and followed immediately by the price. Hodgson is signalling that he knows the convention and is not going to spend the book on it.

quotations.text: the readers will but shake their heads, and be the more convinced that I was mad
quotations.context: On why he is writing the diary at all.
quotations.analysis: He anticipates his audience and writes anyway. The sentence also establishes that he expects to be gone when it is read, the first hint that the manuscript will outlive him.

quotations.context: Emerging from a chasm in the first vision.
quotations.analysis: The scale changes without warning and the prose does not raise its voice. Hodgson's method in the visionary chapters is to describe impossible geography in the tone of a walking guide.
quotations.source: 1908 text, The House in the Arena

quotations.text: a stupendous structure built apparently of green jade
quotations.context: The building at the centre of the arena.
quotations.analysis: One material, one colour, and the sentence that follows makes it his own house. The vision offers no interpretation, and the book's refusal to gloss its central image is the reason the image has survived a century.
quotations.source: 1908 text, The House in the Arena

quotations.text: in no particular, save in color and its enormous size, did the lonely structure vary from this house in which I live
quotations.context: Realising what he is looking at.
quotations.analysis: The clause is careful, legalistic and slightly clumsy, which is how a frightened man checks a fact. What it establishes is that the house is duplicated somewhere else, which goes well beyond a haunting, and nothing in the novel ever qualifies that.
quotations.source: 1908 text, The House in the Arena

quotations.text: It was the face of a swine.
quotations.context: Looking down into the chasm at the first of the creatures.
quotations.analysis: Six words, full stop, no adjective. After pages of careful approach Hodgson gives the reveal the shortest sentence available, and the plainness is what makes it land.
quotations.source: 1908 text, The Thing in the Pit

quotations.text: he literally and actually crumbled into a mouldering heap of bones and dust
quotations.context: Nudging the sleeping dog with a foot, during the acceleration of time.
quotations.analysis: The adverbs are doing something unusual: literally and actually are a man refusing to be thought metaphorical. It is also the moment the cosmic chapters acquire a cost, because the reader was told on page one what the dog was worth.

quotations.context: Standing over what is left of Pepper.
quotations.analysis: Four words for a friend. The diminutive is what hurts, and it is also the book's measure of scale: against a dying sun, a life is a small heap on a study floor.

quotations.text: it was imperative she should leave me, before the Sun of Darkness
quotations.context: The woman explaining why she must go as the white orb is eaten across.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is hers, not his, and it is the only piece of vocabulary the book borrows from beyond. A sun that is darkness is a contradiction the novel does not resolve; it simply arrives again, larger, in the final chapters.
quotations.source: 1908 text, The Noise in the Night

quotations.text: the pen has trailed away over the paper; possibly, through fright and weakness
quotations.context: The last footnote, on the unfinished word that ends the manuscript.
quotations.analysis: The book closes on a note about handwriting, not a vision. After the death of the sun, the editor's evidence-based caution — possibly, through fright and weakness — is the most frightening sentence in it, because it is the only one that sounds reasonable.

timeline.label: Hodgson born in Essex
timeline.detail: The son of an Anglican clergyman who moved the family thirteen times; two of his brothers died young.

timeline.label: Hodgson goes to sea as an apprentice
timeline.detail: Apprenticed at thirteen after a first attempt to run away; eight years at sea gave him the horror of the ocean that runs through all his work.

timeline.label: Hodgson opens a gymnasium in Blackburn
timeline.detail: He left the sea, opened a gymnasium in Blackburn and photographed storms; the discipline shows in his fiction's practicality.

timeline.label: Hodgson's first novel, The Boats of the Glen Carrig
timeline.detail: His first novel, published the year this one was written.

timeline.label: Author's introduction dated 17 December 1907
timeline.detail: The author's introduction is signed December 17, 1907.

timeline.label: Published by Chapman & Hall
timeline.detail: Reviewers admired the siege and were baffled by the cosmic chapters.

timeline.label: Hodgson's The Night Land published
timeline.detail: His last and longest novel takes the end-of-the-sun material of this book and builds a whole world on it.

timeline.label: Hodgson killed at Ypres
timeline.detail: He enlisted at thirty-seven, was invalided out, re-enlisted, and was killed by a shell in April 1918.

timeline.label: Lovecraft praises the novel in Supernatural Horror in Literature
timeline.detail: Supernatural Horror in Literature calls the novel's cosmic sweep a classic of the first water and begins its rescue.

timeline.label: Arkham House reprint
timeline.detail: The House on the Borderland and Other Novels put Hodgson back in print in America and fixed his reputation.

places.note: The kind of western Irish country the fictional Kraighten is set in, reached by a road that stops.

places.name: The Burren, County Clare
places.note: Limestone country full of sinkholes and underground rivers, the geology the pit is drawn from.

places.name: Blackburn, Lancashire
places.note: Where Hodgson ran his School of Physical Culture and began writing.

places.name: Borth, Ceredigion
places.note: The Welsh coast where he lived while writing his novels.

places.name: Ypres, Belgium
places.note: Where he was killed in 1918, ten years after this book appeared.

criticalViews.position: The first cosmic horror novel in English
criticalViews.summary: The second half abandons plot, character and consequence to watch the solar system end, and every later writer who put human beings against indifferent time is working in its shadow.
criticalViews.counter: Its cosmology is Edwardian, not modern: entropy as spectacle, with gods in an arena. The visionary chapters are as much religious as scientific.

criticalViews.summary: A competent siege story and an extraordinary cosmic reverie sit side by side, and readers regularly prefer one and skip the other.
criticalViews.counter: The siege buys the reverie its credit: the reader trusts the man watching the sun die because he was exact about doors, ammunition and a cellar slab.

criticalViews.summary: Hodgson is repetitive, fond of capitals and given to constructions no editor would pass; the book is admired in spite of its sentences.
criticalViews.counter: The stiffness is built into the fiction — the editor warns of it on the first page — and the plainest sentences in it, the face of a swine and the little hill of ash, are the ones nobody forgets.

essayQuestions.question: What does the frame narrative allow the novel to do?
essayQuestions.focus: Found manuscripts, damage and the right to stop
plan: Describe the frame: anglers, a ruin, a damp book, an editor who declines to interpret.
Show how the document's condition licenses the gaps in the story.
Examine the footnotes, and the way their confidence rises as the events become less explicable.
Take the final note about the pen trailing off as the book's real ending.
Argue for what would be lost if the Recluse simply told his story.

essayQuestions.question: How do the two halves of the novel depend on each other?
plan: Set out the siege: creatures, barricades, ammunition, a sister kept ignorant.
Set out the cosmic chapters: acceleration, the green star, the dead sun.
Show what the first half establishes about the narrator's reliability and precision.
Use Pepper as the hinge: comic relief during the siege, and the heaviest loss by the end.
Decide whether the book is two stories or one argument.

essayQuestions.question: Why is nothing explained?
essayQuestions.focus: Withheld cause, and what it does to a reader
plan: List what the novel never answers: the pit, the creatures, the arena, the jade house.
Contrast the gothic convention, where a secret is eventually produced.
Consider the editor's footnotes as the text's own attempt at explanation, and their failure.
Weigh the effect on a reader: frustration, or a dread that survives the last page.
Conclude on what later writers took from the refusal.

discussionQuestions: The Recluse calls himself not superstitious on the page before the visions begin. Does the book agree with him?
Why does Hodgson make the house's double green jade, and never say more about it?
The swine-things are never connected to the cosmic material. Should they have been?
Is Pepper's death the most affecting moment in the novel, and if so what does that say about it?
The editor's last note explains a pen. What is he refusing to say?
Would the ending work at all without the siege that comes before it?

related.why: Published a year earlier, and the other English story of its decade about a place where something else presses through.
Hodgson's own ghost-finder, taking the same practicality — measurements, defences, evidence — into six short cases.
Wells in the same decade, taking the other route out of the Victorian novel: an indifferent intelligence arrives, where Hodgson has a universe running down.
The earlier account of a solitary man writing down what he has seen, and expecting not to be believed.
A siege told through documents, and the measure of how much apparatus Hodgson does without.
